newsitem.title: USA: Gantt closing with Helms in U.S. Senate bid.
newsitem.headline: Gantt closing with Helms in U.S. Senate bid.

text.p: North Carolina Democrat Harvey Gantt, vowing to unseat Republican Sen. Jesse Helms, fought to win over undecided voters Monday as polls showed him closing in on his archconservative opponent.

A CBS News poll Friday showed a statistical dead heat, with Gantt at 47 percent and Helms 45 percent. This followed a poll by the Mason-Dixon group last week that had Helms leading Gantt 49 percent to 42 percent, with 9 percent undecided.
The Mason-Dixon poll had a margin or error of 3.5 percentage points, while the CBS poll had a margin of error of 4 percentage points.

With just two weeks to go before the voting, a rerun of the 1990 contest between the two men, Gantt spent Monday morning trying to win over undecided workers and senior citizens in central North Carolina.
Stumping at a textile factory in Albermarle, he stressed "old-fashioned values and new ideas" that he hopes will help to win over voters and end Helms' 24-year Senate career.

He discussed a $10,000 college tuition tax deduction for working families and used the issue of equal pay for women to characterise Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, as out of touch with voters' concerns.

Gantt, 53, said he supported equal pay because women often earned at least half their family's income. He charged that Helms, 75, did not see a discrepancy in salaries for women and men despite studies showing women made one-third less. "Maybe the senator doesn't understand this because he's just been in Washington too long," Gantt said.
Aides for the Helms campaign did not return calls on the poll data or the Nov. 5 election.
"It's a changing world for working familes and North Carolina needs a senator who understands it," said Gantt, an architect and two-time mayor of Charlotte. He was the city's first black mayor.
While the two candidates have not even met let alone debated in this or the previous race for the U.S. Senate, they have traded barbs in television advertisements.

Gantt's ads say he supports the things that Helms opposes: tax cuts for the middle class, protection of student loan programmes, Medicare and pensions. They tell voters Helms favours tax breaks for the rich and companies that move jobs overseas.
Helms' ads have focused on the hot-button issues of homosexuality and welfare, charging Gantt supported same-sex marriage and higher spending for welfare.

David Paletz, a political science professor at Duke University, said polls rarely captured the real support for Helms. "There are people in the state who end up supporting him (but) who tell pollsters they're undecided," he said.

But Paletz said Helms was "incredibly vulnerable" because more than 686,000 new voters, many also new to the state, were hearing more about Helm's record of anti-communism, segregation, and opposition to abortion and gay rights.

"Helms is vulnerable to a principled attack which tells people about those aspects to his record to which they would object. Up to this time I have not seen that coming from Gantt effectively," Paletz said.

Race, which became the turning point in the 1990 contest, has not become a big issue so far this year. In 1990, Helms and Gantt fought a close race that Helms won narrowly after using controversial television ads suggesting that Gantt would take jobs away from whites and give them to blacks.
